summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for crash_2, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: Baseline viscoelastic evidence of hyperfibrinolysis on point-of-care testing modifies treatment benefit because antifibrinolytic tranexamic acid stabilizes formed fibrin clots and reduces ongoing hemorrhage and mortality.

Baseline viscoelastic evidence of fibrinolytic shutdown modifies treatment harm because tranexamic acid may prevent necessary fibrin turnover and promote pathologic clot persistence, increasing arterial and venous occlusive events.

Long delay from injury to presentation (>3 hours) modifies treatment harm because delayed tranexamic acid administration occurs after the early hyperfibrinolytic phase and may exacerbate thrombotic risk as fibrinolysis wanes.

Concurrent intracranial haemorrhage or severe traumatic brain injury modifies treatment effect because intracranial hyperfibrinolysis contributes to progressive bleeding that tranexamic acid can limit, whereas fibrinolytic shutdown may increase ischaemic cerebral complications.

Pre-injury therapeutic anticoagulation modifies treatment effect because impaired thrombin generation and altered coagulation biochemistry reduce fibrin formation so tranexamic acid alone may fail to restore haemostasis and could shift the balance toward thrombosis once coagulation recovers.

Thrombocytopenia on admission modifies treatment benefit because inadequate platelet-driven clot formation limits the substrate for antifibrinolytic stabilization, reducing the haemostatic efficacy of tranexamic acid.

Biochemical coagulopathy on presentation (prolonged PT/INR) modifies treatment benefit because deficient fibrin network formation undermines the capacity of tranexamic acid to preserve clot integrity and control bleeding.

Severe acidosis on admission modifies treatment effect because acid-mediated suppression of coagulation enzymes reduces fibrin formation and may limit the efficacy of tranexamic acid while altering thrombosis risk.

Requirement for massive transfusion on arrival modifies treatment benefit because ongoing consumptive coagulopathy and active fibrinolysis in massively bleeding patients increase the likelihood that targeted tranexamic acid will reduce mortality and transfusion, whereas untargeted use could expose patients without hyperfibrinolysis to unnecessary risk.

History of prior venous thromboembolism modifies treatment harm because a baseline prothrombotic phenotype may predispose to thrombus propagation and recurrent venous occlusion when fibrinolysis is inhibited by tranexamic acid.

Pregnancy at baseline modifies treatment effect because the physiologic hypercoagulable state of pregnancy may amplify thrombotic risk from tranexamic acid in the absence of demonstrable hyperfibrinolysis.

Delayed or absent surgical haemorrhage control at the time of tranexamic acid administration modifies treatment benefit because antifibrinolytic clot stabilization is transient and without definitive source control persistent bleeding or rebleeding will negate mortality benefit and prolong transfusion needs.

Severe hypovolaemic shock on arrival (marked hypotension or elevated lactate) modifies treatment benefit because shock-associated systemic fibrinolytic activation makes antifibrinolytic therapy more effective at controlling bleeding and reducing transfusion requirement.

Marked hypothermia at baseline modifies treatment effect because temperature-dependent impairment of platelet function and coagulation enzyme activity alters fibrinolytic dynamics and may blunt or unpredictably shift the balance of benefit versus thrombotic harm with tranexamic acid.

Advanced age with known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease modifies treatment harm because pre-existing endothelial dysfunction and a procoagulant vascular milieu increase susceptibility to arterial occlusive events when fibrinolysis is suppressed.
